entry.title: Speculative Encoding: Many-to-Many Cache Translation (24 minute read)
entry.content:
Agents are increasingly passing context to one another as text. Speculative encoding translates hidden states directly from one model to another. It makes the model start answering faster than prefilling the text while keeping most of its accuracy. Prefill costs grow quadratically with context length, and prefill repeats much of what the sending model has already computed.

entry.title: Swarms do not yet raise the roof (46 minute read)
entry.content:
Swarm-based LLM configurations, coordinated groups of agents, deliver faster but less efficient results compared to single agents at equal token budgets. Adding more agents to a swarm introduces a performance penalty that grows with size, leading to quality degradation. Experiments reveal that previous "swarm premiums" result from single agents becoming stale over time. Given fresh context resets, single agents outperform swarms, suggesting that current swarm strategies primarily accelerate compute rather than significantly enhancing capabilities.

entry.title: What VP ≠ VNP Means (3 minute read)
entry.content:
The Anthropic proof that VP≠VNP means that there is no way to find the permanent of a matrix of 0s and 1s if we are limited to arithmetic circuits of size polynomial in the input-size. This means that for P to equal NP, there must be some trick to computing permanents using AND/OR/NOT on the bits of the input that is better than addition and multiplication. There are many problems where access to Boolean operators is helpful, but it isn't clear how they would help with the permanent. There is a $1 million prize for a solution to this problem.

entry.title: Recursive Self-Editing: LLMs Program Their Own Weight Edits for Self-Improvement (1 minute read)
entry.content:
Today's language models improve themselves through data, training recipes, or scaffolds. Whenever their weights change, gradient descent writes the update, not the model. SELFWRITE lets the model write its own weights. Each generation, the current model studies its own reasoning on fresh training problems, inspects its own weights and activations in a persistent Python session, and writes a program that constructs a low-rank weight edit for itself from white-box primitives. It can raise gate accuracy and accuracy on a held-out test split that the loop never sees without a single gradient step.

entry.title: Eliminating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference with Integer-Only Arithmetic (15 minute read)
entry.content:
A floating-point number stores a fixed number of significant digits and a separate exponent. When two numbers with very different exponents are added, the small one has to be shifted to line up with the big one, and the digits that fall off on the end are gone. That means that (a+b)+c is not always equal to a+(b+c). This post looks at what happens when integer addition, which is exact, is used.
